Abstract
Artificial intelligence weather prediction (AIWP) has achieved strong performance in pointwise
accuracy and tropical cyclone track forecasting, yet many models substantially underestimate
cyclone intensity and exhibit deficiencies in physical consistency. These limitations constrain
their use in research-oriented atmospheric simulations. We develop a regional AIWP framework
for the western North Pacific that combines a multiscale mesh, a broad set of atmospheric and
surface variables, and a message-passing graph neural network with linear attention.
Predictability-dependent filtering and spectral constraints are introduced during training to
mitigate excessive smoothing and preserve mesoscale variability. Relative to a model trained
solely with pointwise mean squared error, the spectrum-aware variants improve tropical cyclone
intensity forecasts as verified against ERA5 while largely preserving track accuracy, at the cost
of a modest increase in pointwise error. Structural diagnostics also show improved
representations of inner-core dynamics and thermodynamic structure. In 30-day autoregressive
integrations with ERA5-derived lateral boundary forcing, the models retain organized cyclone
circulations and remain stable in most cases despite not being explicitly trained for these longer
horizons. Stronger spectral retention is accompanied by a modest reduction in long-term
stability. These results demonstrate the value of spectrum-aware training for improving tropical
cyclone forecasts and support further investigation of its use in extended atmospheric simulations
and other extreme weather applications.

Plain Language Summary
Artificial intelligence can produce accurate weather forecasts, but its predictions often
underestimate tropical cyclone strength and blur mesoscale atmospheric features. These
shortcomings limit its use in studying how storms evolve. We develop a regional weather model
for the western North Pacific that uses a broad set of atmospheric and surface variables. We also
adjust how the model learns from its errors so that it balances forecast accuracy with the
preservation of atmospheric features across different spatial scales. This approach improves
forecasts of cyclone intensity relative to the reference reanalysis while largely maintaining track
accuracy. It also produces storm circulations and temperature structures that more closely
resemble those in the reference data. In monthly simulations supplied with boundary conditions
from reanalysis, the models can retain organized storms, although preserving stronger mesoscale
variability can reduce stability. These results suggest a way to improve AI-based cyclone
forecasts and support longer atmospheric simulations, while highlighting the need to evaluate
performance under realistic forecast boundary conditions.

1 Introduction
Tropical cyclones (TCs) are among the most destructive weather systems, causing substantial
economic damage and loss of life worldwide. Predicting TC track, intensity, and structure
remains a major forecasting challenge. Reliable forecasts are essential for anticipating TC-related
hazards and supporting risk assessment and preparedness (Powell & Reinhold, 2007). Alongside
advances in high-resolution, physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP), data-driven
models have become increasingly important in weather forecasting. These approaches span
applications ranging from statistical post-processing and downscaling to global autoregressive
models capable of producing medium-range forecasts.

Data-driven weather forecasting has advanced through several distinct modeling paradigms.
Early graph neural network–based systems demonstrated forecast skill approaching that of state-80
of-the-art NWP models, despite operating at relatively coarse spatial resolution (Keisler, 2022).
Subsequent studies demonstrated competitive medium-range forecast skill using markedly
different architectures, including adaptive Fourier neural operators (Pathak et al., 2022),
hierarchical three-dimensional Transformer architectures (Bi et al., 2023), and multiscale graph
representations. Progress has also depended on training methods and data strategies. GraphCast
combined multiscale representations with multi-step rollout training (Lam et al., 2023), whereas
Aurora leveraged heterogeneous data and large-scale pretraining to extend data-driven prediction
across multiple Earth-system applications (Bodnar et al., 2025). Together, these developments
show that diverse architectures can achieve high forecast skill and underscore the importance of
training strategy, objective formulation, and data composition (Garg et al., 2026). Consequently,
further advances in AI weather prediction may depend not only on model architecture but also on
the properties of atmospheric variability that training objectives encourage models to retain.

Although data-driven weather prediction models have substantially improved conventional
verification metrics, including root-mean-square error (RMSE) and anomaly correlation
coefficient (ACC), these metrics provide only a partial characterization of forecast quality
(Zhang et al., 2026). Such aggregate accuracy measures may obscure important forecast
deficiencies, including systematic underestimation of TC intensity, biases in storm structure and
cross-scale variability, and increasingly oversmoothed forecast fields at longer lead times (L. A.

Smith & Thorpe, 2026). These deficiencies can substantially limit the practical value of data-100
driven models for TC forecasting. Despite competitive track forecasts, data-driven models still
lag behind operational guidance in TC intensity forecasting (DeMaria et al., 2025; Liu et al.,
2024). This gap is particularly pronounced for extreme events that require generalization beyond
commonly observed conditions, including super typhoons and TC rapid intensification (Chih et
al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025).

The training objective may contribute to these deficiencies, particularly excessive smoothing and
underestimated intensity. Most deterministic data-driven weather prediction models are trained
primarily to minimize pointwise mean squared error (MSE). However, the conditional mean that
minimizes expected MSE does not necessarily correspond to a physically realizable atmospheric
state. As forecast uncertainty increases, the conditional distribution broadens, and its mean may
increasingly average over multiple plausible atmospheric evolutions rather than represent an
individual realization (Selz et al., 2026). For spatially varying weather systems, such averaging
can attenuate sharp gradients and small-scale structures, thereby producing progressively
smoother forecast fields. A spectral perspective further clarifies this limitation. In a spherical
harmonic representation (assuming orthonormalized basis functions), MSE can be decomposed
into contributions associated with differences in spectral amplitude and phase (Bouallègue,

Spatial displacement of a forecast feature appears spectrally as a phase change. Even when the
amplitude of a displaced feature is accurately reproduced, pointwise verification penalizes the

forecast both where the observed feature is absent from the forecast and where the displaced
forecast feature appears. This is the double-penalty effect of pointwise verification. As a
feature’s location becomes more uncertain, reducing its amplitude can lower the expected
pointwise squared error by reducing the penalty for misplaced high-amplitude structures.
Pointwise MSE optimization can therefore favor reduced forecast activity as predictability
decreases, a behavior commonly described as the accuracy–activity trade-off (Bouallègue, 2024).

Consistent with this mechanism, several AI weather prediction systems exhibit reduced spectral
variability relative to reanalysis, particularly at smaller spatial scales and longer forecast lead
times. This tendency can become especially pronounced in models trained with multi-step
autoregressive rollouts (Philippé et al., 2025), even though autoregressive curriculum training is
commonly employed to improve forecast accuracy and long-term stability (Bodnar et al., 2025;
Lam et al., 2023). For TC prediction, improved model design may improve predictability and
mitigate excessive smoothing; however, substantial biases remain in the representation of inner-144
core structure and dynamics (Weng & Gori, 2026). These include deficiencies in TC intensity,
wind–pressure relationships, radial wind structure, radius of maximum wind, and dynamical
balance. Together, these results suggest that improvements in conventional forecast accuracy do
not necessarily imply improvements in TC structure and dynamics.

These limitations motivate training objectives that explicitly account for spectral properties.
NeuralGCM, for example, incorporates lead-time-dependent spectral filtering together with
spectral amplitude and bias constraints within its deterministic training formulation (Kochkov et
al., 2024). Other approaches include the binned spectral power (BSP) loss, which constrains the
distribution of power across spatial scales (Chakraborty et al., 2026), and the adjusted mean
squared error (AMSE), which separates spectral amplitude errors from decorrelation errors to
reduce the incentive for excessive smoothing (Subich et al., 2025). These approaches provide a
foundation, but preserving spectral power alone does not ensure accurate feature placement,
realistic TC structure, or consistent relationships among variables. Moreover, spectral
formulations developed for global domains, particularly those based on spherical harmonics,
must be adapted to limited-area regional grids and boundary-forced prediction systems.

A central question is whether preserving spectral variability in a fully data-driven regional model
improves TC intensity and structure, and at what cost to pointwise forecast accuracy. Addressing
this question requires more than improved power spectra: spectral fidelity must be evaluated
together with pointwise forecast error and TC-specific structural diagnostics.

We investigate this accuracy–variability–structure trade-off using a fully data-driven regional
deep-learning framework for the western North Pacific. We develop a regional graph neural
network using ERA5 reanalysis and a controlled training framework for comparing spectral
objectives with conventional pointwise optimization (Hersbach et al., 2020). The model
combines multiscale graph representations with a broad set of atmospheric and surface variables,
and the training procedure progressively extends forecast lead time and introduces predictability-172
dependent spectral filtering and constraints on spectral variability. We evaluate whether these
objectives improve TC representation using three complementary classes of diagnostics:
conventional pointwise verification, spectral measures of atmospheric variability, and TC-175
specific measures of track, intensity, and storm structure. This design tests whether greater
spectral activity is accompanied by physically meaningful improvements in simulated storms.

Section 2 describes the data and methodology. Section 3 outlines the evaluation framework.
Section 4 evaluates model performance using synoptic-scale metrics. Section 5 presents tropical
cyclone verification, including track, intensity, and storm structure. Section 6 presents case
studies and extended-range simulations. Section 7 discusses the main findings, limitations, and
implications.

2 Data and Methodology
2.1 Dataset
The dataset is constructed from ERA5 reanalysis data on a 0.25° latitude–longitude grid
(Hersbach et al., 2020). We use a regional rather than global domain to limit computational cost
while retaining sufficient interior area for evaluating predictive skill. The temporal subset
includes periods extending three days before and after times when a TC’s best-track position lies
within the domain. This selection reduces the number of samples by approximately half while
retaining the atmospheric evolution during and around TC lifetimes. The data are divided into

separate training, validation, and test sets, with all reported evaluations based on the 2024 test
set. Three-dimensional atmospheric variables are represented on 13 pressure levels.
Climatological reference fields used for selected evaluation metrics are obtained from
WeatherBench (Rasp et al., 2024), and TC positions and best-track information are obtained
from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) best-track dataset and IBTrACS v4. Dataset
details are summarized in Table 1.

To better represent atmospheric interactions, we include a broader set of variables than the
simplified dynamical fields used in previous studies. This choice reflects the coupled physical
processes governing TC evolution, including oceanic energy supply (Emanuel, 1986), boundary-204
layer angular momentum transport (R. K. Smith & Montgomery, 2025), eyewall replacement
cycles, and terrain-induced potential vorticity changes (Wang, 2012; C.-C. Wu & Liao, 2026).
These interactions are also relevant to TC genesis, during which cloud–radiative feedbacks (Hsu
& Wu, 2025), mid-level vorticity (Loi et al., 2024), and other environmental conditions may
jointly determine whether an incipient disturbance organizes into a mature TC (Tseng et al.,
2026). Including variables associated with these processes provides a broader physical basis for
learning coupled TC evolution. The variables used in this study are summarized in Table 2.
All fields are sampled at six-hour intervals. For all accumulated variables, the values represent
accumulations over the preceding one-hour interval. Missing sea surface temperature and
significant wave height values are replaced by 270 K and 0 m, respectively. During data
preprocessing, spatial nearest-neighbor filling is applied to sparse missing surface values, and
bilinear interpolation is used to map wave height onto the atmospheric grid. Temporal inputs
include the local-solar-time ratio, the annual-phase ratio, and the sine and cosine transforms of
both quantities. Predicted SST and wave height are fed back as inputs at subsequent
autoregressive steps within the domain interior, whereas lateral boundary values are prescribed
from ERA5.

2.2 Graph Representation and Model Architecture
An appropriate spatial representation is essential for modeling atmospheric evolution. Numerical
weather prediction models use configurations including nested domains in WRF and variable-225
resolution meshes in MPAS-A to allocate computational resources to regions that require finer
resolution (Park et al., 2014). In this study, the ERA5 fields are provided on a regular 0.25°
latitude–longitude grid. Although the angular grid spacing is uniform, the physical spacing varies
with latitude because meridians converge toward the poles (Figure 1a and 1b). We therefore
distinguish between the grid on which atmospheric inputs and predictions are defined and the
graph representation on which latent features are processed.

Existing AI weather prediction models employ different spatial representations and
computational architectures. Pangu-Weather and Aurora use three-dimensional architectures
derived from the Swin Transformer (Bi et al., 2023; Bodnar et al., 2025), whereas the spherical
Fourier neural operator approach developed for FourCastNet processes atmospheric fields in the
spectral domain (Bonev et al., 2023). Here, we adopt an icosahedral graph representation similar
to that used in GraphCast (Lam et al., 2023). Unlike GraphCast, which combines connections
from multiple refinement levels into a multimesh graph, we retain each refinement level as a

separate graph. This design processes latent atmospheric features at distinct spatial resolutions
and exchanges them through explicit interlevel connections.

Graph neural networks process information through message passing between connected nodes
(Battaglia et al., 2018). In our formulation, edge features are updated from the states of
connected nodes, and the resulting messages are aggregated to update node states. Encoding
relative geometry in the edge features allows these updates to account for both atmospheric
conditions and the spatial relationships between interacting locations. This mechanism supports
learning of spatially coupled dynamics, consistent with previous applications of graph neural
networks to physical simulation (Pfaff et al., 2020; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020).

The graph hierarchy comprises five icosahedral refinement levels (3–7), containing 38, 156, 618,
2,441, and 9,749 nodes, respectively (Figure 1e–i). Together with the latitude–longitude grid,
these meshes form a heterogeneous graph with distinct node types and connectivity patterns. To
reduce truncation of graph neighborhoods near the lateral boundaries, mesh nodes are retained
over an extended domain with a 2.5° buffer around the atmospheric grid (Figure 1c and 1d). The
buffer supplies additional nodes for connections near the domain edges without enlarging the
atmospheric prediction domain.

Separate connectivity rules govern encoding, processing, decoding, and information exchange
between mesh levels. During encoding, grid nodes are connected to level-7 mesh nodes within a
prescribed great-circle distance to transfer atmospheric information from the regular grid to the
mesh (Figure 1j). Within each mesh level, processor edges connect adjacent mesh nodes and
include self-loops; Figure 1k illustrates a level-7 node connected to its six neighbors and itself.
During decoding, each grid node receives information from its three nearest mesh nodes at the
relevant refinement level to project learned mesh features back onto the latitude–longitude grid
(Figure 1l).

Successive mesh levels exchange information through pooling and upsampling connections in a
graph U-Net structure (Gao & Ji, 2022). These connections link coarse-level nodes to seven-269
node neighborhoods on the finer mesh. Pooling aggregates fine-level information onto the

coarser mesh, whereas upsampling transfers coarse-level information back to the finer mesh. 271 Together with message passing within each level, these operations combine information across 272 spatial resolutions.

Each graph neural network layer exchanges information within the first-order neighborhood

single-head attention. Their outputs are combined through a learnable sigmoid gate, followed by
layer normalization. Each level has a separate gate parameter initialized to 0.5, giving an initial
local-branch weight of approximately 0.622.

We incorporate several components to improve graph-based learning and training stability,
including edge features, normalization, dropout, residual connections, feed-forward networks,
and positional encodings (Luo et al., 2024, 2025). Layer normalization supports stable training
with relatively small batch sizes (Ba et al., 2016). A gated linear unit replaces the conventional
feed-forward network to provide feature-dependent gating and nonlinear feature transformations.

2.3 Training
Training proceeds in four stages to balance forecast accuracy and physical consistency. Stage 1
pretrains the model on a coarser mesh, and Stage 2 fine-tunes it on a finer mesh. Stage 3 extends
training from single-step predictions to multistep autoregressive rollouts. Stage 4 adds
predictability-dependent filtering and spectral losses to the objective. This progression moves
from learning the large-scale environment to resolving finer-scale features, maintaining stability
over longer integrations, and preserving the distribution of spectral variability.

The training hyperparameters are summarized in Table 3. Prediction targets are formulated as
atmospheric-state increments. Loss weights account for latitude-dependent grid-cell area and the
relative importance and predictability of different variables.

The treatment of lateral boundary conditions (LBCs) is important for regional autoregressive
models because boundary errors can propagate into the interior through advection or wave
propagation (Warner et al., 1997). In numerical models using semi-Lagrangian advection, for
example, the lateral boundary buffer must span several grid points to support numerical stability
(Davies, 2014). In our configuration, ERA5 lateral boundary forcing is applied over a nine-grid-358
point buffer beginning at the second autoregressive step.

The predictability-filtered MSE objective is designed to retain accuracy at predictable scales
while reducing the incentive to excessively damp spectral variability. The spectral-error loss
constrains the distribution of variability across scales, and the spectral-bias penalty limits
systematic drift. Together, these terms are intended to improve the physical consistency of
autoregressive rollouts.

We compare the MSE-only baseline with two spectrum-aware variants that penalize absolute or
squared spectral errors. For fixed normalization, squared-error gradients increase with error
magnitude, whereas absolute-error gradients remain constant away from zero. However, the
variants differ in both norm and normalization. Their comparison therefore evaluates the
combined formulations. Spectra are computed using a planar Fourier approximation of the
regional domain, with radial wavenumber binning under an assumption of statistical isotropy.
3 Evaluation
All evaluations use the 2024 test set, following the tropical-cyclone-centered sampling criterion
described in Section 2.1. Forecasts are initialized at 00, 06, 12, and 18 UTC. We evaluate three
variants of the proposed model: the Stage 3 checkpoint trained solely with the weighted MSE
objective and two Stage 4 variants incorporating the Spectrum-MAE and Spectrum-MSE
formulations, respectively.

For external comparison, Pangu-Weather serves as a deterministic reference (Bi et al., 2023).
Although more recent deterministic AI weather prediction systems, such as GraphCast and
Aurora (Bodnar et al., 2025; Lam et al., 2023), have demonstrated improved performance in
conventional global forecast metrics, including RMSE, Pangu-Weather is useful for the

objectives of this study. It offers lower computational overhead, and previous studies have
extensively examined its tropical cyclone forecasts, providing context for interpreting our results
(DeMaria et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024; Weng & Gori, 2026). Furthermore, Pangu-Weather does
not employ the multi-step autoregressive curriculum training commonly adopted in later systems
and has been reported to exhibit less progressive smoothing during extended autoregressive
rollouts (Philippé et al., 2025). Its comparatively moderate spectral dissipation makes it a useful
reference for evaluating whether the proposed spectrum-aware objectives can retain mesoscale
spectral variability and improve the physical consistency of the forecast fields, rather than merely
reducing conventional pointwise forecast errors.

Although the nine-grid-point boundary buffer is excluded from verification, prescribed ERA5
boundary forcing can still influence the interior domain during autoregressive integration.
Accuracy metrics from the second forecast step onward therefore characterize a boundary-443
constrained regional system and do not constitute a comparison with Pangu-Weather under
identical information constraints. Accordingly, Pangu-Weather serves as an external reference,
while the effects of spectrum-aware training are assessed primarily by comparing the three
variants of the proposed model under the same lateral boundary conditions.

respectively (Bonavita & Geer, 2026). Together, these metrics help determine whether the
spectrum-aware objectives improve the representation of atmospheric variability without
substantially degrading conventional forecast accuracy. The corresponding formulations are

To characterize the scale dependence of forecast variability, we analyze the Fourier power
spectra of the forecast and reference fields using isotropic radial binning. These diagnostics
identify the spatial scales at which forecast variance is attenuated or amplified relative to ERA5,
complementing forecast activity, which measures overall variability without resolving its
distribution across scales. They show whether mesoscale variability is retained throughout the
forecast but do not directly diagnose energy transfer between scales.

For TC verification, we adopt a TC tracker similar to that in Aurora (Bodnar et al., 2025),
augmented with a weighted-centroid algorithm. The cyclone center is identified primarily using
the minimum mean sea level pressure (MSLP). Over land, where MSLP-based tracking may
become less reliable, the 700-hPa geopotential-height field is instead used to determine the
cyclone center. Linear extrapolation from the preceding track positions stabilizes center selection
and reduces unrealistic jumps between consecutive forecast times. Only cases satisfying a
minimum TC intensity threshold of 35 kt in the JTWC best-track maximum sustained winds are
retained for verification.

To maintain a common sample, TC verification includes only cases available in all four model
configurations, including the external Pangu-Weather baseline. JTWC best-track positions must

lie at least 5° inside the domain boundaries, and geographic filtering is applied separately to each
model’s forecast center before selecting cases common to all four models. These restrictions
reduce the direct influence of prescribed lateral boundary information on the verification results.
To limit the effects of small sample sizes, TC verification is restricted to lead times of 72 h or
less.

5 Tropical Cyclone Verification
To assess the impact of spectral-loss training on TC) forecasts, we apply the TC tracking
algorithm described in Section 3 and evaluate forecasts using a common-sample framework. To
maintain comparable samples as TCs enter or leave the domain, develop, or dissipate, we retain
only cases successfully identified in all four model configurations. The evaluation is conducted
at lead times of 1, 2, and 3 days, with 265, 211, and 162 forecast samples, corresponding to 18,
16, and 15 individual TCs, respectively.

Spectral-loss training improves TC intensity prediction while largely preserving track accuracy
(Figure 7). Absolute track errors differ only slightly among training objectives, consistent with
the dominant influence of large-scale environmental steering on TC motion. In contrast, TC
intensity is more sensitive to the representation of mesoscale structures. Consistent with the
improved retention of mesoscale spectral energy, the spectral-loss models reduce intensity errors
relative to both the MSE-only baseline and Pangu-Weather under the present evaluation
framework.

Spectral-loss training also improves the distribution of TC intensity changes. In particular, the
spectral-loss models better reproduce the upper tail of the ERA5 intensity-change distribution,
whereas pointwise-loss forecasts tend to underrepresent strongly intensifying cases. Preserving
this tail behavior is especially relevant for forecasts of rapid intensification, for which excessive
smoothing of mesoscale structures may systematically suppress large intensity changes. These
results link improved mesoscale spectral retention translates into more accurate representations
of storm intensity and intensification.

6 Case Studies and Extended-Range Simulations
The preceding synoptic-scale and tropical cyclone diagnostics provide an aggregate assessment
of how spectrum-aware training affects forecast variability, intensity, and storm structure. We
next examine an intense TC case and month-long simulations to assess performance in a high-696
impact event and during extended integration. The first experiment focuses on Typhoon Krathon
(2024), while the second examines model stability and spectral characteristics during month-long
autoregressive simulations.

Figure 11 compares the track and intensity evolution of Typhoon Krathon in the forecasts,
ERA5, and the best-track record. Krathon moved westward through the Bashi Channel in late
September and early October 2024 while rapidly intensifying to Category 4 intensity on the
Saffir–Simpson scale. The storm subsequently decelerated and nearly stalled before turning
northeastward and making landfall over southwestern Taiwan. During the period of peak
intensity, Pangu-Weather substantially underestimates the storm intensity, whereas the regional
model variants more closely reproduce the intensity evolution in ERA5. Although the spectrum-707
aware variants produce slightly stronger storms than ERA5 near peak intensity, their stronger
intensification and higher peak intensity are closer to the substantially stronger JTWC best-track
record. The best-track wind maximum occurs approximately one day after the ERA5 S10
maximum. Thus, their higher intensity relative to ERA5 may partly reflect the reanalysis’s
limited effective resolution rather than simply an excessive intensification bias. However, this
comparison remains qualitative because the model and ERA5 S10 maxima differ in temporal and
spatial representation from the JTWC 1-minute maximum sustained winds.

The spatial forecast fields further illustrate these differences. Figure 12 shows the evolution of
850-hPa wind speed and 700-hPa specific humidity during the first three forecast days. In Pangu-717
Weather, the specific-humidity fields exhibit noticeable grid-like artifacts, which may reflect its
patch-embedding architecture. In contrast, the graph-based models produce smoother spatial
transitions without the same rectangular artifacts. The spectrum-aware models retain stronger
winds on the right side of the storm track, resulting in a more distinct asymmetric wind-field
structure. Their moisture fields also preserve sharper variations in the rainband environment,

including clearer boundaries between moist and relatively dry regions. These features become 723 increasingly distinguishable with forecast lead time.

To assess whether these differences persist beyond conventional medium-range forecast
horizons, we conduct month-long autoregressive simulations for 96 initial conditions. Initial
conditions are selected at regular intervals from the 2024 test set, requiring continuous data
coverage for the preceding input and the full forecast period. Both initialization dates and all
verifying times fall within 2024. Each simulation is run for up to 30 days while retaining ERA5-739
derived lateral boundary forcing. Simulations producing NaNs or exhibiting extreme numerical
growth are excluded in their entirety from the aggregate spectra, yielding a constant number of
contributing runs across the reported lead times. Figure 13 and Figure 14 summarize the
evolution of spectral energy during these simulations for 700-hPa specific humidity and 850-hPa
wind. Among the retained simulations, the Spectrum-MSE model consistently retains a larger
fraction of the reanalysis spectral energy than the Spectrum-MAE model throughout the 30-day
integrations. The separation between the two models generally increases with forecast lead time.
The enhanced spectral-energy retention of the Spectrum-MSE model is accompanied by a
modest reduction in long-term numerical stability. Of the 96 initial conditions, four Spectrum-748
MSE simulations become unstable, compared with one for the Spectrum-MAE model. These
results suggest a trade-off between retaining higher-frequency variability and limiting the growth
of forecast perturbations over extended integration periods.
For a qualitative examination of the month-long simulations, we select the forecast initialized at
00 UTC on 21 October 2024. This period is characterized by active tropical cyclone genesis over
the western North Pacific, providing a test of whether the models retain realistic structures over
several weeks. As shown in Figure 14, both spectrum-aware models continue to simulate
organized tropical cyclone circulations at integration times approaching 27 days. The simulations
exhibit repeated cyclone development, intensification, and dissipation rather than progressively
collapsing toward an excessively smooth background state.
Differences between the two spectral-loss formulations are evident in the spatial fields.
Consistent with the spectral diagnostics, the Spectrum-MSE model maintains stronger mesoscale
variability in both the moisture and wind fields. Tropical cyclone circulations are generally more

intense, and the surrounding specific-humidity fields exhibit sharper spatial gradients than in the 762 Spectrum-MAE simulation. One possible explanation is the difference in error weighting 763 between the spectral objectives. For fixed normalization, the magnitude of a squared-error loss 764 gradient increases with spectral error, assigning stronger corrections to spectral components with 765 large amplitude discrepancies, whereas an absolute-error loss does not exhibit this error-766 dependent amplification. Differences in normalization may also contribute. 767 These experiments complement the aggregate verification. The Krathon experiment 768 demonstrates that spectrum-aware training improves the representation of an intense and 769 compact tropical cyclone, particularly its wind intensity, asymmetric circulation, and moisture 770 structure. The month-long experiments show that the spectrum-aware models retain mesoscale 771 variability during extended, boundary-forced autoregressive integration. At the same time, the 772 comparison between the Spectrum-MAE and Spectrum-MSE variants indicates that stronger 773 spectral-energy retention can come at the cost of reduced long-term stability. These results 774 therefore suggest that spectral-loss design influences not only forecast sharpness but also the 775 balance between mesoscale variability and autoregressive stability.

In the monthly simulations, the spectrum-aware models sustain the development and evolution of
multiple TCs under reanalysis-derived lateral boundary forcing. This retention of organized
circulations supports their potential use in extended, boundary-forced simulations, but does not
establish unconstrained long-range forecast skill.

The comparison between the two spectral-loss formulations does not identify a consistently
superior formulation, particularly because their normalization schemes differ. Nevertheless, the
results reveal distinct characteristics. Under their respective normalization schemes, the
Spectrum-MAE configuration better preserves medium-range forecast accuracy and high-808
wavenumber features in short- and medium-range forecasts, whereas the Spectrum-MSE
configuration more effectively retains the overall spectral-energy distribution during month-long
autoregressive integrations, at the cost of greater degradation in conventional accuracy metrics
and reduced long-term stability. This contrast further illustrates the trade-off between pointwise
forecast accuracy and the preservation of dynamically relevant variability and consistency
(Bouallègue, 2024). Future work could combine these objectives or transition between them
across forecast time scales. More broadly, these results underscore the importance of training
objectives and data alongside model architecture (Garg et al., 2026).

Several limitations qualify these findings. The regional simulations remain constrained by
reanalysis-derived lateral boundary forcing. Consequently, the experimental framework is more
comparable to a regional WRF-style simulation than to a fully operational forecasting system,
limiting direct comparisons of absolute forecast accuracy with global operational models. In
addition, the primary references for TC intensity and structural diagnostics are derived from
reanalysis. The reanalysis does not fully resolve the most intense and compact TC inner cores,
introducing uncertainty into the evaluation. The diagnosed improvements therefore primarily
describe agreement with ERA5 within the present regional, boundary-forced configuration.

Despite the benefits of spectral training, the framework still depends on manually specified
choices. Future work should assess and reduce sensitivity to the filter cutoff wavenumber, the

relative weights of the loss components, and the weights assigned to different forecast variables.
It will also be important to test whether these effects depend on model architecture or generalize
across AIWP systems. Moreover, the aggregate verification covers only one test year, leaving the
robustness of these findings across years and under out-of-distribution conditions to be
established.

An important next step will be to replace reanalysis-derived lateral boundary conditions with
forecasts from global prediction systems and evaluate the resulting sensitivity to boundary
uncertainty. The TC evaluation framework could also be extended to other high-impact weather
systems, such as atmospheric rivers and other mesoscale extremes. Overall, spectrum-aware loss
functions provide a promising means of reducing excessive smoothing and improving the
representation of TC intensity, variability, and structure in deterministic AI weather prediction.
